To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the exchange rate rule is superior to the money supply rule when the variance of innovations is small, but the money supply rule is superior to exchange rate rule when the variance is large.
the variability of output is larger in the presence of a variance-dependent parameter than it would be in its absence.

the variability of output in an open economy is lower under a money supply rule than under an exchange rate rule when the variance of innovations in aggregate demand and market specific innovations are sufficiently small.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: How do variance-dependent parameters in a macro model influence the variability of output and the choice of the optimal rule?
the effects of the variance-dependence of the slope of the Phillips curve on the performance of monetary and exchange rate rules.
the effects on output variability of the variance of innovations in the aggregate supply curve and the variance of innovations that affect the exchange rate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
when the variance-dependent parameters are sufficiently large, the exchange rate rule is superior to the money supply rule.
, in the presence of variance-dependent parameters and when variances are sufficiently high, the exchange rate rule dominates the money supply rule in terms of output stabilization.

when the variances of demand and exchange rate innovations are small, the money supply rule dominates the exchange rate rule, while the opposite is true if the variances of these innovations are large.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results of our paper suggest that a monetary rule may dominate an exchange rate rule in terms of the variance of output when the variance of market-specific innovations is small, but an exchange rate rule may dominate a monetary rule when the variance of innovations is sufficiently large.
the results obtained for a constant slope of the aggregate curve are reversed when the variances of market-specific innovations are large enough to affect the slope of the curve.

the variance-dependent parameter approach is useful for analyzing output variability and that it is not possible to draw general conclusions about the relative merits of money supply and exchange-rate rules without considering the variance-dependence of the slope of the supply curve.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the variance dependence of parameters can lead to counterintuitive results.
the variance of the slope of the supply curve may be large enough to reverse the ranking of rules in terms of their ability to stabilize output.
the choice between money and exchange rate rules is not as clear cut when the variance of innovations is large.
